1:1.t: That in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, son of Hystaspes, the seventieth year of the desolation of the temple, which Jeremiah had prophesied, was completed, the prophet Zechariah is also a witness: for when he had set at the head of his vision the title, in the second year of the same king, in the eleventh month, Shebat, on the twenty-fourth day, he added, saying: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? This is the seventieth year. And Ezra too, when only the altar had been built and the foundations of the temple laid, relates that the work was forbidden by the letters of King Artaxerxes: Then the work of the house of God in Jerusalem was interrupted, and it was not done until the second year of the reign of Darius, king of the Persians. […]

In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on day one of the month, the word of the Lord came in the hand of Haggai the prophet. Because the people, who seemed to themselves to have returned from captivity, had not yet built the temple nor raised the walls of the city, nor had it the glory of the former Jerusalem, but dwelt in hollow houses, and, as it is said more expressively in Greek, κοιλοστάθμοις, that is, set low down and sunk in a valley; for that reason the word of God comes to them not under King Hezekiah, or Amon, or Josiah, who had ruled the people of God as long as Jerusalem stood, but under King Darius, prince of the Persians, of whom Daniel too speaks mystically in his volume. Now Darius sounds in our language 'generations made', or 'which have been', which in Greek is said γενεαὶ γενομέναι; […]

See, then, that our very works cry out to the Lord while we ourselves are silent. Therefore it is said: "The word of the Lord came in the hand of the prophet Aggeus." It does not come to him in his mouth, that is, in speech, but in his hand, that is, in work. "For the kingdom of God is not in speech" but in the hand, that is, in work.

And hands are interpreted as works. Whence it is written: 'The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai,' 'The word which came by the hand of Jeremiah the prophet.' Surely the word of the Lord does not come by the hand, but comes in the mouth. But see the mysteries of Scripture. God does not come to speech, except to good works. For a murderer too confesses Christ, and yet the Lord does not come to him, because his hands do not deserve the Lord's coming.

Wherefore then is it in their hands, not in their tongues? “And swords,” it saith, “sharpened on both sides in their hands.” By “in their hands,” he meaneth in power. They received then the word of God in power, to speak where they would, to whom they would, neither to fear power, nor to despise poverty. For they had in their hands a sword; where they would they brandished it, handled it, smote with it: and all this was in the power of the preachers. For if the Word be not in their hands, why is it written, “The Word of the Lord was put in the hand of the Prophet Haggai”? Surely, brethren, God set not His Word in His fingers. What is meant by, “was put in his hand”? It was put into his power to preach the Word of the Lord.

1:2.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts, saying: This people says: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built. Note carefully that it is not Zerubbabel or Joshua who say: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built, but the people, which, still placed under King Darius, had not yet shaken off the yoke of servitude. And always those who are held in captivity, and have gone out of Jerusalem, put off and delay building the temple of God, and say: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built. And you, when you see someone who has gone out of the Church, who had been delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved, thinking and planning to build through chastity the temple which he had before destroyed through lust, and yet putting it off from day to day, say to him: Truly you too are of the people of the captives; you too say: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built. […]

1:3.t: And the word of the Lord came in the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Is it a time for you to dwell in panelled houses — or, as the LXX translated: Κοιλοστάθμοις, that is, hollow —, and this house deserted? On the same day as above, this vision is seen again. And as the works of the prophet advance, the gifts of prophecy also grow; and after a little silence, to what the people had said: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built, the Lord's response, as if thought over, is brought forth, and it is said to them: Is it then time for you to dwell in houses set low down and placed in a valley, and shall my house, which is on the mountain, be deserted? Or, as it stands in the Hebrew: That you should dwell in panelled houses, that is, adorned and well arranged, and which serve not so much for use as for delight; and shall my dwelling, in which were the holy of holies, and the Cherubim, and the table of the showbread, be drenched by the rains, lie squalid in desolation, be scorched by the sun? […]

1:5.t: And now thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways. Let there not be one time for speaking and another for doing; turn my precepts at once into deeds. For it is the Lord Almighty who commands, and surely the command of God Almighty is no light thing. Until now you have had hearts that served vices, without order, without a teacher, going wherever your desires dragged them. But now the Lord commands you to set charity in order toward him, and to set your hearts upon your ways, so that you do nothing without judgment and consideration, but the lamp of the law always goes before your feet, and you say: Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. Or certainly thus: Because you say, it is not the time for building the house of the Lord, and you yourselves dwell in dwellings sunk in the depths, while my house is deserted, consider, at my command, the Lord's, and call back to your memory what you have done and what you have suffered.

1:6.t: Generally speaking, riches that are not under complete control are the citadels of evil. If the ordinary people look on them covetously, they will never enter the kingdom of heaven, because they are letting themselves become contaminated by the things of this world and are living above themselves in self-indulgence. Those concerned for their salvation should take this as their first principle, that, although the whole of creation is ours to use, the universe is made for the sake of self-sufficiency, which anyone can acquire by a few things. They who rejoice in the holdings in their storehouses are foolish in their greed. "He that earned wages," Scripture reminds us, "put them into a bag with holes." Such is the man who gathers and stores up his harvest, for by not sharing his wealth with anyone he becomes worse off.

You have sown much, and brought in little; you have eaten, and have not been satisfied; you have drunk, and have not been inebriated; you have covered yourselves, and have not been warmed. And he who gathered wages put them into a bag with holes. All your labor, you who built your own houses and neglected the house of God, has had no result. For you sowed more, and gathered much less than had been sown; nor can you say that famine followed because the farmer ceased from working the land. You ate too, lest perhaps any of you should say that the fast had been voluntary; and you were not filled, because you had gathered small fruits into your barns. You drank wine from the vineyards, but not so much that your heart was gladdened and it could be said of you: And wine gladdens the heart of man. You had a cloak, but one that would neither keep off the cold nor keep in the warmth. Whoever of you, too, gathered wages, whether by trade or by hired hand, spent his labor in vain, without the price of the labor. […]

And in these allusions and inconveniences all that are at all weak are sure to be entangled, as while they are even doubtful of their own salvation, and themselves stand in need of the teaching and instruction of others, they are incited by the devil's tricks to convert and guide others, and as, even if they succeed in gaining any advantage from the conversion of some, they waste by their impatience and rude manners whatever they have gained. For that will happen to them which is described by the prophet Haggai: "And he that gathereth riches, putteth them into a bag with holes." For indeed a man puts his gains into a bag with holes, if he loses by want of self control and daily distractions of mind whatever he appears to gain by the conversion of others. And so it results that while they fancy that they can make larger profits by the instruction of others, they are actually deprived of their own improvement.

1:7.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways; go up into the mountain, bring wood, and build the house; and it shall be acceptable to me, and I shall be glorified, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Set your hearts on your ways; go up upon the mountain and cut down wood. The rest likewise. Again I, the Lord, command you, I who had also ordered it before, that you set your hearts upon your ways, and consider all that you do, and, leaving off your zeal for your own lowly houses, go up into the mountain, where there is not wood to be burned, but wood that serves for the works of my house; and so that you may do this more attentively, know that what you are doing will please me. The Hebrews say that only wood for roofing was needed, since the walls of the temple were left standing after the fire. So they say. But we are commanded not to set our hearts outside our ways, but to set again in our ways the hearts we had set before; […]

1:8.t: Neither does he build a sepulchre for himself who dies before the time, for "he is dead while he liveth;" and he hears not the voice of Haggai, that is being interpreted, of the Feaster, for he enters not the Tabernacle of God, "in the voice of praise and thanksgiving, the sound of one feasting." For how can he hear His voice, who sees not His works? If he saw them, he would have heard the Word which has been put in His Hand, rejoicing in His acts, whereby "He knocked and it was opened to Him," and He descended into his soul that He might feed therein upon the food of sincerity and truth. Now because he has not heard, the word of Haggai comes again to hand, and says, Rise up from your "cieled houses" that are weighed down by wickedness, and "go up to the mountain" of the heavenly Scriptures, and "hew wood," the wood of wisdom, the wood of life, the wood of knowledge; and make straight your ways, direct your acts that they may keep their due order which is useful and necessary for building the house of God.

1:9.t: You looked to more, and behold, it became less; and you brought it into the house, and I blew it away. LXX: You looked to many things, and they became few, and you brought them into the house, and I blew them away. So that, casting aside delay and laying down all hesitation, you may build my house more zealously, I tell you also another thing that has befallen you, who put off building my house: not as above, You have sown much, and because the earth did not return the seed, you have brought in little; but when the crops were already whitening, and the time of harvest was at hand, and you thought you held the grain in your hands, you reaped empty stalks and gathered hollow straw without the fruit of the ears. The threshing floors were full: hope in the eyes, grief in the hands. But even this very thing which had scarcely been picked out of the great crop and the countless heaps, you brought into the house, and it was scattered by my power. […]

1:10.t: Because of this, over you the heavens were forbidden to give dew, and the earth held back its growth. Not only, he says, did the heavens not give rain, by which the watered soil produces crops, but not even the morning and the night dew, so that the parched fields might at least be tempered by a little moisture. The earth too devoured, and, not meaning to return the seed to the farmers, held back in its greedy bosom even what it is accustomed to produce of its own accord. I think that this is the dew of which it is said to Jacob in the blessing: May God give you of the dew of heaven; and the dew of Hermon which descends upon Mount Zion, and descends not from the air, in which flits a manifold number of eagles and hawks and vultures, but from heaven, so that if anyone's soul burns with passions and has been wounded by the dart of the devil, it may be cooled by this dew and temper its heats. When this is withheld, the earth also does not bring forth its growth. […]

1:11.t: And I called a drought upon the earth, and upon the mountains, and upon the wheat, and upon the wine and upon the oil; and whatever the ground brings forth, and upon men and upon beasts, and upon all the labor of hands. For drought the Seventy translated μάχαιραν, that is, sword; but in the Hebrew too I found it written with three letters, heth, res, beth, which, if we read harseb, means sword; if oreb, καύσωμα, which we have translated drought, although it could better be translated burning wind. And indeed, since the discourse is about the earth and about the barrenness of the fields, it seems to me that burning wind ought rather to be understood in the present place than sword, although every plague that is brought upon men for their sins can also be taken for a sword. Now a drought, or a sword, was called upon the earth and upon the mountains, so that they should not bring forth wheat, and wine and oil, and whatever the ground produces of its own accord. […]

1:12.t: And Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the great priest, and all the remnant of the people heard the voice of their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God sent him to them, and the people feared before the face of the Lord. Attend carefully (because of the two understandings of the Savior in Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the priest, for he himself is both king and priest) to this: that he did not say, Zerubbabel and Joshua feared; but when Zerubbabel and Joshua and the people heard the words of Haggai the prophet, which are the words of the Lord, the people alone feared before the face of the Lord, that is, the multitude alone, which had not yet come into one and perfect man, and which, not joined to the spirit, did not merit to be what the spirit is. But the people feared before the face of the Lord, knowing that the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.

1:13.t: And Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, from among the messengers of the Lord, spoke to the people, saying: I am with you, says the Lord. Some think that John the Baptist, and Malachi, which means angel of the Lord, and Haggai, whom we now have in hand, were angels, and that by the dispensation and command of God they took on human bodies and lived among men. Nor is it surprising that this should be believed of angels, since for our salvation even the Son of God took on a human body; and for this reason they also offer testimony from the apocrypha, where it is said that Jacob, who was afterwards called Israel, was an angel, and that for this reason he supplanted his brother in his mother's womb; also that John, at the voice of Mary, the mother of the Lord, leapt for joy in the womb of Elizabeth; and that all rational beings have one nature, and that for this reason men who have pleased God become equal to the angels. Let them think so. […]

1:14.t: And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the great priest, and the spirit of the rest of all the people; and they went in and did work in the house of the Lord of hosts, their God. On the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius. For governor of Judah the Seventy translated, of the tribe of Judah, and for work, works; the rest likewise. But wherever we put: the Lord of hosts, they variously render either the Lord Almighty, or the Lord Sabaoth, or the Lord of powers. So the spirit of Zerubbabel is stirred up, and the spirit of Joshua, for the present according to the letter, so that the kingdom and the priesthood may build the temple of God. The spirit of the people is stirred up too, which before was sleeping in them: not the body, not the soul, but, as we have said, the spirit, which knows better how to build the temple of God. […]

2:1.t: So the word of God comes to those who had begun to work in the house of the Lord Almighty, now in rest, that is, in the seventh month and in the most complete mystery of the Trinity, on the twenty-first of the month, and to Haggai, who was celebrating the feasts of God and had again prepared his hand for the word of the Lord, and he says to him: Speak to Zerubbabel of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua the great priest, who for our sake deigned to become both man and priest, and to the remnant of the people; for in comparison with the whole world, the part of those who believed was small in the beginning.

In the seventh month, on the twenty-first of the month, the word of the Lord came in the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the great priest; and to the rest of the people, saying: Who is left among you that saw this house in its first glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not so, as if it were not, in your eyes? And now take courage, Zerubbabel, says the Lord, and take courage, Joshua, son of Jehozadak, great priest, and take courage, all people of the land, says the Lord of hosts, and do it. For I am with you, says the Lord of hosts. The word that I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt, and my spirit will be in your midst; do not fear. For thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet there is one little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, and the sea and the dry land, and I will move all nations. And the one desired by all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. […]

2:3.t: Let us therefore hear what he said. There was once in Israel a house of God, which is now so deserted that it is not even believed to have existed, since she who had been beloved became not beloved, and they who were not the people of God began to be the people of God. And that house, once glorious, is now in the sight of Zerubbabel and Joshua and the remnant of the people as if it were not. And we ought to take this not only of the buildings of the temple, which we see have collapsed, but of all the things which the Jews once had as glorious.

2:4.t: In the next place, he was stripped of his former solid raiment and adorned with a garment down to the foot, and with a turban and a clean miter, that is, [with the garb] of the second advent; since he is demonstrated as having attained "glory and honor." [Since stripped] you will not be able to say that the man [there depicted] is the "son of Jehozadak," who was never clad in a sordid garment but was always adorned with the sacerdotal garment, nor ever deprived of the sacerdotal function.

Whoever scans all the books of the prophets, both of the twelve and of the others, will find many testimonies regarding the Holy Spirit. Haggai says, "For I am with you, says the Lord of hosts, and my spirit continues in your midst."

Nevertheless, because the former house has become as if it did not subsist, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the priest are roused, so that the kingdom and the priesthood of Christ may be strengthened, and his people, which was once the people of the land, may do works in the house of the Lord and know that God is present to it.

2:5.t: Let it also do the word which the Lord covenanted with them when they were coming out of the land of Egypt. And would that we too may come out of Egypt, so that we may fulfil the word of the covenant which we have received. The Lord God also promises his spirit to those who do works in his house and fulfil the word they have received, saying: And my spirit will be in your midst. Behold the mystery of the Trinity: I am with you, and my Spirit, and the Word, in which I set the covenant when you came out of Egypt. But what he says, in your midst, is to be understood in the sense of what we read written in the Gospel: For he stands in your midst, whom you do not know, who will come after me.

2:6.t: "Yet once more," I hear the Scripture say that the heaven and the earth shall be shaken, inasmuch as this has befallen them before, signifying, as I suppose, a manifest renovation of all things. And we must believe S. Paul when he says that this last shaking is none other than the second coming of Christ, and the transformation and changing of the universe to a condition of stability which cannot be shaken. And I imagine that this present shaking, in which the contemplatives and lovers of God, who before the time exercise their heavenly citizenship, are shaken from us, is of no less consequence than any of former days.

These things, then, says the Lord of hosts to you who see that the former house is as if it were not. I moved heaven, when my voice was heard from heaven. I moved the earth, when I delivered the covenant to the former people, and at my coming gloom, whirlwind and darkness were seen. I moved the Red Sea, when I provided a way for the people passing over. I moved the dry land, either Egypt, emptied of the worship of God through the plagues, or the wilderness through which I led the people about for forty years. These I will move yet once more. This we see fulfilled in the coming of the Lord the Savior. For at the time of his passion, as the sun fled, heaven was moved, and darkness came over all the earth from the sixth hour until the ninth hour. The earth was moved, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened; the sea was moved, when the dragon that was in it was slain; the dry land too was moved, the once fruitless wilderness of the nations.

2:7.t: And in this trembling of the universe all the nations too were shaken, because into all the earth has gone out the sound of the apostles of the Lord, and their words have penetrated to the ends of the world. And all the nations were moved for this reason, that from their movement the chosen things of the nations might come, and whatever is excellent anywhere. For example, the chosen things from Corinth, because there was much people of God in it; the chosen things from Macedonia, because the great Church of God gathered in Thessalonica had no need to be taught about love; the chosen things from Ephesus, so that they might know the secrets of God and mysteries revealed to none before. Why say more? All the nations were shaken to which the Savior had sent the apostles, saying: Go, teach all nations; and out of the many called, the few chosen built the Church of the firstborn. Hence the apostle Peter too: Greets you, he says, she who is elect in Babylon, and Mark my son; and John: The elder, he says, to the elect lady; […]

There remain for discussion the three minor prophets who belong to the closing days of the captivity, namely, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. To begin with, Haggai has the following brief but clear prophecy of Christ and the church: "For thus says the Lord of hosts: yet one little while, and I will move the heaven and the earth, and the sea and the dry land. And I will move all the nations, and the desired of all nations shall come." It is obvious that this prediction is, in part, already fulfilled; the rest we may confidently expect at the end of the world. Surely God set the heavens rocking when angels and a star stood as witnesses to the birth of Christ; surely too he moved the earth when he performed the tremendous miracle of giving Christ a virgin birth. Surely he moved the sea and the dry land when he made Christ's name known throughout the whole world, on island and on mainland. For the rest, we ourselves are witnesses of the fact that all nations are being moved to accept the faith. […]

2:8.t: Riches, gold and silver, are not the devil's as some think, for "the whole world of riches is for the faithful man, but for the unfaithful not a farthing." But nothing is more faithless than the devil. God through the prophet says plainly, "Mine is the silver, and mine is the gold." Only use it well and there is nothing blameworthy in silver; but when you abuse a good thing and are then unwilling to blame your own conduct, you impiously put the blame on the Creator. One can even be blessed by money. "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat"4—undoubtedly by the use of money; "I was naked and you covered me"—assuredly by the use of money. Consider too that money can be a door to the heavenly kingdom. "Sell," he says, "what you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven."

And as far as the Lord is distant from the servant, so much better is the house of the Lord, over which the Lord presides, than the former house, over which a servant presided. And as for what he says: Mine is the silver, and mine is the gold, says the Lord of hosts, I do not think that anyone supposes that he is speaking of the silver and gold that are possessed by the rich and by kings. For in this way not only silver and gold belong to God as Creator, but also the other metals, bronze, tin, lead, and iron, which tames all things. But I take the silver with which the house of God is adorned to be the utterances of the Scriptures, of which it is said: The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances; silver tried by fire, proved by the earth, purged sevenfold; and the gold to be what dwells in the hidden thought of the saints and in the secret place of the heart, and shines with the true light of God; […]

Surely the glory of the house of the New Testament is greater than that of the old because it was built of better materials, namely, those living stones that are human beings renewed by faith and grace. Yet precisely because Solomon's temple was renovated—was made new—it was a prophetic symbol of the second Testament which is called the New. Accordingly we must understand the words God spoke by Haggai's mouth, "And I will give peace in that place," as referring to the place for which the temple stood. Since the restored temple signified the church, which Christ was to build, those words can mean only "I will give peace in that place [the church] which this place [the rebuilt temple] prefigures." (All symbols seem in some way to personify the realities of which they are symbols. So, St. Paul says, "The rock was Christ," because the rock in question symbolized Christ.) […]

2:9.t:
This our new and excellent Zerubabel, having heard the word which announced beforehand, that she who had been made a desert on account of God should enjoy these things, after the bitter captivity and the abomination of desolation, did not overlook the dead body; but first of all with prayers and supplications propitiated the Father with the common consent of all of you, and invoking the only one that giveth life to the dead as his ally and fellow-worker, raised her that was fallen, after purifying and freeing her from her ills. And he clothed her not with the ancient garment, but with such an one as he had again learned from the sacred oracles, which say clearly, 'And the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.'

Thus, enclosing a much larger space, he fortified the outer court with a wall surrounding the whole, which should serve as a most secure bulwark for the entire edifice. […]

2:10.t: It is to be noted, however, that in this place, On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the second year, it is not said, as it was above for the third time, The word of the Lord came in the hand of Haggai the prophet, but to Haggai the prophet. For there — because he was still making progress and had only clean works, but his heart had not yet received full wisdom, or because he still dwelt among those who said, The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built — the word of the Lord came only in his works. Here, however, since the foundations of the temple have now been laid, and the people with its rulers has entered the house of God and is doing work befitting the temple of God, and has heard the mystery, I will move all the nations, and the one desired by all the nations shall come, and is full of prophecy, therefore the word of the Lord comes wholly to Haggai. Of the twenty-fourth day and the second year we have already spoken. […]

On the twenty-fourth of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests the law, saying: If a man carries sanctified flesh in the border of his garment, and with its edge touches bread, or pottage, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it be sanctified? And the priests answered and said: No. And Haggai said: If one polluted in soul touches any of all these, shall it be defiled? And the priests answered and said: It shall be defiled. And Haggai answered and said: So is this people, and so is this nation, before my face, says the Lord; and so every work of their hands, and all that they have offered there, shall be defiled. […]

2:11.t: For it is not so easy to dye deeply a piece of cloth, or to impregnate with odours, foul or the reverse, whatever comes near to them; nor is it so easy for the fatal vapour, which is rightly called a pestilence, to infect the air, and through the air to gain access to living beings, as it is for the vice of a superior to take most speedy possession of his subjects, and that with far greater facility than virtue its opposite. For it is in this that wickedness especially has the advantage over goodness, and most distressing it is to me to perceive it, that vice is something attractive and ready at hand, and that nothing is so easy as to become evil, even without any one to lead us on to it; while the attainment of virtue is rare and difficult, even where there is much to attract and encourage us. […]

He writes to Timothy, who had been trained in the holy writings from a child, exhorting him to study them diligently and not to neglect the gift that was given him with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. To Titus he gives commandment that among a bishop's other virtues (which he briefly describes) he should be careful to seek a knowledge of the Scriptures: "A bishop," he says, must hold fast "the faithful word as he has been taught that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers." In fact, lack of education in a clergyman prevents him from doing well to anyone but himself, and much as the virtue of his life may build up Christ's church, he does it an injury as great by failing to resist those who are trying to pull it down. The prophet Haggai says—or rather the Lord says it by the mouth of Haggai—"ask now the priests concerning the law." For such is the important function of the priesthood to give answers to those who question them concerning the law.

And at the same time consider that it is the office of priests to answer one who asks about the law. If he is a priest, let him know the law of the Lord; if he does not know the law, he himself proves that he is not the Lord's priest. For it belongs to the priest to know the law and, when questioned, to answer concerning the law. This indeed we read in Deuteronomy too: that if anywhere in the cities of Israel a question should arise between blood and blood, between judgment and judgment, leprosy and leprosy, dispute and dispute, they are to go to the priests and Levites, and to the high priest who shall have been appointed in those days, and ask of him the law of the Lord; and when these have answered, they are to do what they are commanded. But if they do not do it, they are to be cut off from their people. […]

2:12.t: Knowing, then, what sanctified flesh is, and one unclean in soul, let us see what the prophet asks. If any man: here it is not said of the high priest, or of a priest, or of a Levite, but of any man whatever; where no person is specified, all are freely permitted to touch the flesh. If, he says, he carries sanctified flesh and has tied it in the edge of his garment, and the edge of the garment itself touches bread, or any other cooked food, or wine, or oil, or anything besides these on which a man can feed, can the bread or pottage, or wine, or oil or any food be sanctified by the touch of the garment in which the holy flesh is tied? And the priests answered and said: It cannot; that is, none of the things you ask about will be sanctified, but each will remain as it was.

But what is it that Haggai, in the person of the Lord, asks the priests? If a man carries sanctified flesh in the border or in the edge of his garment, and with its edge touches bread, or pottage, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it be sanctified? Before we treat of the question, we ought meanwhile to know, according to the letter, what sanctified flesh is and what one unclean in soul is. As for the victim that was sacrificed on the altar, its flesh was holy, and among these sanctified meats themselves there was much diversity. For some the priests ate in the inner sanctuary of the temple, some their kinsfolk ate at home, some those of the priests who were held to be blemished, some Israelites who had no uncleanness. The full account of this diversity is given in Leviticus. But one was called unclean in soul who had touched the body of a dead man. […]

But according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), the man of the Church who has sacrificed the lamb without blemish and a year old, and has put on Christ, if he takes some of its flesh and ties it in the edge of his garment, and that edge touches the bread of the Scriptures, which strengthens the hearts of believers; or cooked food, the apostolic epistles, which, as it were, cut up the meats of the old law and cook them through and offer them seasoned for eating; or wine, which gladdens the heart of man; or oil, by which the face of the hearer is made cheerful; or any food: the milk on which the Corinthians are nourished, and the herbs on which the weak feed, and other things like these; those to whom they are given will not at once eat them as sanctified. For it is not from their being spoken but from their being received that they sanctify the hearers, because many are hearers of the law and not doers. […]

2:13.t: Again another question is put to the priests, since, that is, they had answered the former one well, and a sort of likeness of the problem is fitted to it, in which an unskilled man could easily slip. For suppose someone does not know the law: just as he answered concerning the sanctified flesh that bread, or pottage, or wine, or oil, or any food is not sanctified, so in this case too he will answer alike and say: One polluted in soul does not defile the things that holy flesh could not sanctify. He asks, therefore, and says: If he who is polluted in soul, that is, who has been made unclean by contact with the dead, touches any of all these, namely bread or pottage, or wine, or oil, or the other foods, will the things he has touched be polluted by contact with them? And the priests answered, whose chief was Joshua son of Jehozadak, whence they also knew the law, and they said that by the touch of him who is unclean all things touched by him are polluted.

2:14.t: And Haggai answered and said, passing over in silence the earlier point, that sanctified flesh cannot sanctify the other foods, and weaving the occasion of his discourse from the second question alone: So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord. He who is unclean in soul and has touched a carcass, everything he touches and whatever he offers to me will be unclean. What he says according to the letter is of this kind: O people, who, with only the altar built and my house in ruins, offer me sacrifices on the altar and think that you are sanctified by its victims and its flesh, know that you are not so much sanctified by the sacrifices, which, with the temple in ruins, can be of no profit to you, as that all your works and everything you do are defiled, from the fact that you are negligent and have striven to build your own house rather than mine. What is offered on the altar is indeed holy; […]

2:15.t: Moreover, according to tropology, it is said also to us who now believe in Jesus Christ, if indeed we believe and show its truth by the work of faith, that we should return in mind to that time when we were Gentiles, daily serving vices, and had not built in ourselves a temple to God. And as an architect and most skilled mason joins stone to stone, and cements the lower to the upper with lime and plaster, so also the architect — whom the Apostle too says he is, As a wise architect I have laid the foundation, and whom the Lord threatens that he will take away from Jerusalem — knows how to join works to works and little by little to build up the temple of God. And the foundation of this temple is laid: Jesus, upon whom let each one see what he builds. One builds gold, silver, precious stones; another wood, hay, stubble. And to the three goods three evils are opposed on the contrary side. […]

And now set your hearts from this day and upward, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord. When you came to a heap of twenty bushels, and they became ten, and you went in to the winepress to press out fifty jars, and they became twenty. I struck you with burning wind, and with blight and hail all the works of your hands, and there was none among you who would return to me, says the Lord. LXX: And now set upon your hearts from this day and upward, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord, you who were, when you put twenty measures of barley into the cypsele, and they became ten measures of barley; and you went in to the winepress to draw fifty amphoras, and they became twenty. I struck you with barrenness, and with corruption of the air, and with hail, all the works of your hands; and you did not return to me, says the Lord. […]

The Hebrew explained the whole tenor of this passage, from what is written, And now set your hearts from this day and upward, up to the place where he says, The vine and the fig and the pomegranate, and the olive tree has not flowered: from this day I will bless, in this way: Certainly the foundations of the temple have now been laid; from this day, therefore, on which you laid the foundations — although in the past I punished you with barrenness, and famine, and hail, and drought, and there was none of you who returned to me through these plagues — set your hearts toward the future and onward, and see that all things flow for you on a prosperous course. And this will come about because you have begun to build my temple, and do not, putting your trust in the altar alone, despise the building of my house. […]

2:16.t: When you came, he says, to a heap of twenty bushels, and they became ten: Or, according to the LXX: When you put twenty bushels of barley into the cypsele, and they became ten bushels of barley. For whatever virtues and good works we seemed to have before Christ was not wheat but barley; and that very barley did not, according to our hope and prayers, yield a hundredfold harvest, as we read of Isaac, but we could barely find in it half of our labor, and it was said to us: Have you suffered so many things without cause? But also, when we went in to the winepress and reckoned on fifty amphoras of wine — a number which, when seven weeks are completed, the unity of the Godhead closes — and thought that we had wine, which gladdens the heart of man, the holy number thirty was taken away from us — the number at which the Lord is baptized, and Ezekiel sees his vision at the beginning of his prophecy, and, according to the Hebrew, the priests came to the ministry of God — and twenty were left. This number Esau loves; […]

2:17.t: For there follows: I struck you with burning wind and with blight and hail all the works of your hands. And whatever is struck by blight and hail and burning wind is reduced to dust and ashes, and nothing is found in it that serves for use or for food. All these things indeed the Lord did, because there was not found among them one who would return to him. But if they return and build the temple of the Lord, from the day on which they begin to build they will have what the word of the prophecy goes on to add.

2:18.t: For he remembered that the Lord spoke through Haggai, that on the twenty-fourth of the ninth month, from the day on which the temple of the Lord Almighty was founded, the vine he says and the figs and the pomegranates and the olive trees, which will not bear fruit, from this day I will bless. By this it is revealed that just at the setting of the declining year, that is, at the sunset of an age already growing old, the holy temple of God, which is the Church, was to be founded, by whose grace, through the sanctification of the washing, the peoples of the Jews and of the nations can have the fruit of their merits.

The ninth month is the one we call November or December. For Nisan is the first month among the Hebrews, which is called the month of new things, at the time when they keep the Passover, that is, at the first beginning of spring; following the course of the moon it often occupies some part of the month of March, and sometimes it begins in April. So if we understand Nisan as April, the ninth month by the reckoning of the Hebrews will be December. So it is the tenth month, at the time when the seeds lie hidden in the earth and future fruitfulness cannot be guessed.

That the ninth month is not taken in a good sense, both the fourth book of Kingdoms (2 Kings) and the history of Jeremiah relate, in which Jerusalem is said to have been besieged. Yet since the foundations of the temple are laid at the end of the ninth month, we can understand this: that the building of the temple of the Lord is not begun unless evil works come to an end. Hence also on the twenty-fourth day of the same month the foundation of the temple is laid; in this number there are a double δωδεκὰς (dodecad), and three ὀγδοάδες (ogdoads), and four ἑξάδες (hexads), of which we have already discussed more fully above.

Set your hearts from this day and into the future, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid, set upon your heart. Is the seed already in the sprout, and have the fig and the vine and the pomegranate and the olive tree still not flowered? From this day I will bless. LXX: Set your hearts from this day and into the future, from the four and twentieth of the ninth month, and from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid, set in your hearts. If the threshing floor will any longer be known upon the earth, and if still the vine and the fig and the pomegranate, and the olive trees that do not bear fruit? From this day I will bless. I have set forth to you, he says, what you endured before you began to build my temple; now I will set forth what prosperity is to come to you, because you have begun to build my temple. […]

2:19.t: Is the seed, he says, already in the sprout? This is better said in Hebrew, in the husk, so as to signify the sheath of the grain. Have the vine and the fig, and the pomegranate and the olive tree given their flower? So that from the flower the fruit too may be understood. Certainly not; for in the month of December, as we have said, there are no signs of the crops to come. So that you may not say, then, that I conjecture this by shrewd reasoning and surmise the future fruitfulness from the flowers of the trees and the blades of the crops: behold, there are no signs, and yet, because you have begun to build my temple, I foretell to you a fruitfulness of all crops at my blessing. This we have said according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy the sense is far different, and this too we must first explain according to the letter, so that afterwards the course of tropology we have begun may be treated. […]

Whoever, therefore, has dedicated himself to the worship of God, and has despised the ῥάθυμον, that is, the negligent patron, who in the volume of Ezra, according to the Seventy translators, forbids the temple of God to be built, he does not know the measure of his crops and of his reward. Or certainly, on account of what is said, If the threshing floor will still be known upon the earth, he who has sown in the spirit and from the spirit has reaped eternal life will by no means store up treasure for himself on earth, but all his works and the rewards of his works will be gathered in the heavens. The vine also, that is, the word of God, whose husbandman in each one is the Father; and the fig, the sweetest gifts of the Holy Spirit; and the pomegranate, the doctrines of the Church and the knowledge of the Scriptures, which is compared to the cheeks of the bride in the Song of Songs; and the olive trees will give refreshment and illumination of heart to him who has begun to build the temple of God. […]

2:20.t: It is to be noted, moreover, that on the same day, that is, on the twenty-fourth of the ninth month, with the number of the month passed over in silence because the prophecy concerned the coming of Christ and his kingdom, the word of our Lord comes a second time to Haggai: not in his hand, as before, nor to Haggai the prophet, as in the fourth vision, but simply to Haggai, that is, to one celebrating the feasts of the Lord. For he was to announce and to behold him not as one who would come at some time, but as one coming. And as Abraham saw the day of Christ and rejoiced, and John pointed out the Lamb of God with his finger, so he too, seeing the kingdom of the Son of God, was to have within himself all the solemnities.

And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying: I will move heaven and earth alike, and I will overturn the throne of kingdoms, and I will crush the strength of the kingdom of the nations; and I will overturn the chariot and its rider; and the horses and their riders shall go down, each man by the sword of his brother. On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will take you, O Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and I will set you as a signet, because I have chosen you, says the Lord of hosts. In the LXX there is added: The sea and the dry land, and it lacks: I will crush the strength of the kingdom of the nations, which will be recognized more fully from reading their text.

2:21.t: On this passage most interpreters hold differing opinions: for some suppose that it is said of his first coming; others, of the second, when he is to come in his majesty. We accept both, because he both reigned then, when he came, and is to reign hereafter. Yet if we wish to take it of the end of the world, we shall say what the Apostle says to the Corinthians: To destroy every principality and every power and virtue, that God may be all in all. And because what is said is mystical and pertains to the end of things, the prophet is therefore commanded to speak to Zerubbabel alone, whom we have shown to have come forth as a type of Christ because of the assumption of a body from the seed of David. […]

2:22.t: For this is what he says: And I will overturn the chariot, or chariots, and their riders, and the horses and their riders shall go down. And that you may know that what we have said is signified in the overturning of the chariots and of the horsemen falling headlong, see how it is said of Christ in Zechariah that a gentle king comes, mounting upon a yoke-beast and a young colt of an ass, and destroys the chariots out of Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd, and both hosts, from the nations as well as from the Jews, may be held under a peaceable shepherd. But so that these things which are perverse may be destroyed, each one with the sword — which I take to be the sharpest word of doctrine, cutting away whatever is perverse — will rise up against his brother, cutting off everything opposed.

2:23.t: Wherefore to Him alone is it mystically said, "I will take thee, O Zerubbabel, and will make thee as a signet, for I have chosen thee." When our mind shall have become peaceful so that it may be said to her, "Return, return, O Shulamite," which signifies 'peaceful,' or, to use your own name, Irenice, then shall she receive Christ like a signet on herself, that is, the Image of God, that she may be according to that Image, for "as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly." And it behoves us "to bear the image of the heavenly," that is, peace. And that we may know the truth of this, it is said in the Canticles to the soul now fully perfect, that which may the Lord Jesus say to you also, "Set me as a seal upon thine arm;" that peace may shine in your heart and Christ in your works, and that wisdom and righteousness and redemption may be formed in you.

But the end of all these things is the best. For after the destruction of the thrones, and the strengths of those who reign, and of the chariots and the horses and the horsemen, on that day, says the Lord Almighty: I will take you, Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, my servant. Now he is called servant because of the human body, since then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, and among all things subjected he too will be seen subjected. But when this has been fulfilled, God will set him as a signet in his hand: For him God the Father has sealed; and he is the image of the invisible God and the form of his substance, so that whoever has believed in God may be sealed with him as with a ring.

This Haggai was also privileged to utter predictions concerning the Lord Christ, as, under the person of Zerubabel, he says things which are applicable to the Lord Christ: And I will make thee as a signet, because I have chosen thee, saith the Lord God.
